positions.subject: q:education/sfusd-8th-grade-algebra
positions.summary: Fisher says the evidence supports expanding access to Algebra while keeping Math 8, and that not every student wants to accelerate.

citations.quote: The strongest evidence supports expanding access to Algebra while preserving Math 8 as a critical foundation.
Stanford research and SFUSD pilot data show that offering Algebra as an eighth-grade elective can produce significant gains in both state and local assessment scores

positions.subject: q:education/sfusd-close-or-merge-schools
positions.summary: Fisher says she first opposed closures and objected to the 2024 process, but now favors aligning the number of schools with enrollment to concentrate resources on fewer campuses, with community engagement.

citations.quote: I was initially a vocal opponent of school closures.
Rather, aligning our number of schools and facilities with enrollment could allow us to concentrate resources across fewer, better-resourced campuses and improve the quality of learning environments.
However, no portfolio redesign will be successful without robust engagement and ultimately community buy-in.

positions.subject: q:education/sfusd-proximity-assignment
positions.summary: On Oct. 13, 2026, Fisher voted against Option C, which assigns students to a neighborhood school and limits other applications to citywide programs; KQED reports she supported Option B, which first assigns a neighborhood school and lets families apply to any school with open seats.

citations.quote: Commissioner Alida Fisher, who along with Commissioner Supryia Ray voted no, was concerned about that estimate.

The alternative considered Tuesday, which was dubbed “Option B,” would also have first assigned students to a neighborhood school, but it would have then allowed them to apply to any other school in the district with open seats.
Option B was also supported by board members Alida Fisher and Supriya Ray, who voted against Option C.
She says she wouldn’t accept a system that requires families to give up school choice in exchange for a zone-based model until the district addresses inequities
